content: The MT-TH gene encodes a mitochondrially encoded transfer RNA (tRNA) specific for histidine. This tRNA plays a critical role in protein synthesis by transferring the amino acid histidine to the growing polypeptide chain at the ribosome during translation. The MT-TH gene is located on the p arm of mitochondrial DNA at position 12 and spans 69 base pairs. Structurally, tRNA molecules, including MT-TH, adopt a characteristic cloverleaf shape with three hairpin loops. Mutations in the MT-TH gene are associated with several mitochondrial disorders, including mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes (MELAS), cardiomyopathy, and the MELAS/MERRF overlap syndrome. These mutations can disrupt mitochondrial function, leading to a variety of clinical manifestations. Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, and Stroke-like Episodes (MELAS) A subset of individuals with MELAS has been found to carry mutations in the MT-TH gene. MELAS is a rare mitochondrial disorder that primarily affects the nervous system and brain. Clinical symptoms include recurrent severe headaches, muscle weakness (myopathy), hearing loss, stroke-like episodes characterized by loss of consciousness, seizures, and other neurological complications. MELAS/MERRF Overlap Syndrome MELAS can co-occur with another mitochondrial disorder known as myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibers (MERRF). This combination is referred to as the MELAS/MERRF overlap syndrome. In addition to the symptoms of MELAS, affected individuals may experience muscle twitches (myoclonus), impaired coordination of movement (ataxia), and the presence of abnormal muscle cells called ragged-red fibers. Mutations in the MT-TH gene, such as the 12147G>A mutation, have been implicated in this overlap syndrome. The exact mechanism by which these mutations impair mitochondrial energy production and lead to the observed symptoms remains unclear. A documented case of a patient with the 12147G>A mutation exhibited symptoms including migrainous headache, vomiting, left-sided hemiparesis, lateral homonymous hemianopia, and other features consistent with the MELAS/MERRF overlap syndrome. The patient initially presented with MELAS symptoms, which later progressed to the overlap syndrome. Cardiomyopathy Mutations in the MT-TH gene can also result in cardiomyopathy, a condition characterized by thickening of the heart muscle, particularly in the interventricular septum. This thickening weakens the heart's ability to pump blood effectively. Unlike other mitochondrial disorders, patients with MT-TH mutations causing cardiomyopathy may not exhibit neurological abnormalities or other common signs of mitochondrial disease. A specific mutation, 12192G>A, has been identified in multiple patients with cardiomyopathy, presenting in various forms. The underlying mechanism by which these mutations lead to isolated cardiomyopathy remains unknown. Deafness, Nonsyndromic Sensorineural, Mitochondrial Mutations in the MT-TH gene have also been linked to nonsyndromic sensorineural deafness. A heteroplasmic 12201T>C transition in the MT-TH gene has been identified in a family with varying degrees of sensorineural hearing loss. The onset and severity of hearing loss differed among affected family members.
